extracted.intended_audience: readers of literature and social reformers (advocates against capital punishment)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and authorial choices for composing a literary, persuasive work arguing against capital punishment, exemplified by Victor Hugo's Preface to The Last Day of a Condemned. Focus is on how to frame, structure, and present the condemned's experience to move readers and influence judges/society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare the work as a general plea against capital punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Last Day of a Condemned is only a pleading, direct or indirect, for the abolition of punishment by death.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the central purpose explicit: the work should function primarily as an argument for abolition rather than as a special defence of an individual case. The political/social aim should be foregrounded in the preface or framing material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit specific individual/contingent details to universalize the argument
rubrics_metrics.description: “I have been careful ... to omit any thing of a special, individual, contingent, relative, or modifiable nature, as also any episode, anecdote, known event, or real name,—keeping to the limit ... of pleading the cause of any condemned prisoner whatever.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid real names, particular anecdotes, and temporally or politically contingent specifics so the narrative reads as representative and timeless; this increases the universality and moral force of the plea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place the question where its reality can be seen: the scaffold not the courts
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is the sombre and fatal question ... placed where it should be seen, in its true and hideous position,—not in the law courts, but on the scaffold,—not among the judges, but with the Executioner!”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present the lived, physical reality of capital punishment (scaffold, executioner, crowd) rather than abstract legal argumentation. Show the spectacle and mechanisms of execution to expose its moral horror.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanize the condemned to move readers and judges
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorial aim: to ‘make a heart bleed,’ ‘render merciful those who consider themselves just,’ and ‘penetrate sufficiently deep within the Judge to reach the man.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use first-person interiority, memories, family scenes, and emotional detail to create empathy for the condemned; aim the narrative to pierce institutional detachment and reach readers' conscience and decision-makers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid, sensory, concrete details of the condemned’s last day
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative examples throughout: bells sounding, the cart, crowd behaviour, the Priest’s crucifix, the cutting of hair, the child reading the sentence—sensory particulars of the execution process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ concrete sensory imagery and episode-level description (sights, sounds, physical sensations) to make the reader experience the condemned’s ordeal; specific scenes amplify emotional impact and credibility.
